en: Brahmā was born as the first among the gods,
the creator of the universe and the protector of the world.
He taught the knowledge of Brahman, the foundation of all knowledge, to Atharvan, his eldest son. 1.1.1.
The Brahmā taught that knowledge of Brahman which he had proclaimed to Atharvan;
Atharvan spoke it to Aṅgiras;
and he spoke it to Bhāradvāja Satyavaha.
Bhāradvāja [received] the higher and lower [Veda] from Aṅgiras. || 1.1.2 ||
Śaunaka, a man of great wealth, having approached Aṅgiras in the prescribed manner, asked: "Venerable sir, when what is known does all this become known? (1.1.3)
To him he said: "There are two kinds of knowledge to be known," so indeed say those who know Brahman, "the higher and the lower. 1.1.4.

Therein, the lower [knowledge] consists of the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvaveda, phonetics (śikṣā), ritual manuals (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), prosody (chandas), and astronomy (jyotiṣa). Then, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable (akṣara) is attained. 1.1.5.
That which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, devoid of eyes and ears, and without hands or feet— that is eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, and exceedingly subtle.
That is the imperishable which the wise perceive as the source of all beings. 1.1.6.
Just as a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web],
just as herbs arise upon the earth,
and just as hair and body-hair grow from an existing person.
In this way, the entire universe arises here from the Imperishable. || 1.1.7 ||
Through austerity, Brahman is built up; from that, food is born.
From food arise vital breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and immortality in ritual acts. 1.1.8.
He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge—from him this Brahman, name, form, and food are born. 1.1.9.
Thus ends the first section.
This is the truth:
those rituals which the seers beheld in the mantras were extensively elaborated in various ways during the Tretā age.
Practice those constantly, O you who desire truth;
this is your path to the world of the righteous. 1.2.1.
When the flame flickers in the kindled fire, then one should offer the oblations between the two portions of clarified butter. || 1.2.2 ||
He whose *agnihotra* is without the new-moon sacrifice, without the full-moon sacrifice,
without the four-monthly sacrifices, without the *āgrayaṇa*, and devoid of guests; which is unoffered, without the *vaiśvadeva* rite, or offered contrary to the rule—
It destroys his worlds up to the seventh. || 1.2.3 ||
Kālī, Karālī, Manojavā, Sulohitā, Sudhūmravarṇā,
Sphuliṅginī, and Viśvarucī— the Goddess.
"Leaping about" refers to the seven tongues of flame. 1.2.4.
Those who move among these blazing [fires], duly offering oblations,
are led by these rays of the sun.
Wherein the Lord of the Gods alone is the dwelling place. || 1.2.5 ||
"Come, come!"— thus do the resplendent oblations,
speaking dear words and singing praises, carry the sacrificer away by the rays of the sun.
This is your holy, well-made world of Brahman.
For these forms of sacrifice are but rafts, unstable, consisting of eighteen factors, said to be inferior;
those fools who rejoice in this [as the highest good]...
They return once again to old age and death. || 1.2.7 ||
Existing in the midst of ignorance,
yet considering themselves wise and learned,
the deluded wander about, repeatedly striking themselves down.
Just as the blind led by the blind. || 1.2.8 ||
Existing in various ways within ignorance, fools imagine themselves to have achieved their goal;
because of passion, those engaged in ritual action do not understand this.
Therefore, being afflicted and having their worlds exhausted, they pass away. 1.2.9.
Thinking that sacrifices and charitable works are the highest good, these deluded ones do not know any other excellence.
Having experienced the fruits of their good deeds on the heights of heaven, they enter this world again or even one more degraded. (1.2.10)
Those who dwell in the forest, possessing austerity and faith, peaceful and wise, living on alms—
being free from passion, they depart through the door of the sun.
Wherein that immortal Person resides, whose nature is indeed imperishable.
Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, a Brahmin should arrive at detachment, realizing that "there is nothing uncreated to be gained by what is created.
For the sake of understanding that, he should approach a teacher alone.
With sacrificial fuel in his hand, he should approach a learned Brahmin who is firmly established in the Veda. || 1.2.12 ||
To him who had approached him properly, whose mind was perfectly tranquil and who was endowed with self-control,
that wise one [taught] by which [means] he knows the Imperishable, the True Person.
He taught her that knowledge of Brahman in its true essence. || 1.2.13 ||
Thus ends the second section.
Thus ends the first Muṇḍaka.
This is the truth:
just as from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of the same nature emerge.
In the same way, my dear, from the Imperishable various beings are born, and into it they also merge. 2.1.1.
For that divine, formless Person is indeed both external and internal, unborn;
he is without breath, without mind, pure, and higher than the high Imperishable. 2.1.2.
From this is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs; as well as space, air, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe. (2.1.3)
Agni is his head; the moon and sun are his eyes;
the quarters of space are his ears; his speech is the revealed Vedas;
Vāyu is his breath; and the universe is his heart.
For he, the inner self of all beings, is indeed the earth with his two feet. || 2.1.4 ||
Therefore, Agni is the fuel for him whose sun is Soma; Parjanya [is the rain] from Soma, and the herbs upon the earth;
the man pours his seed into the woman.
Many offspring have been produced from the Puruṣa. || 2.1.5 ||
Therefore, the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, and the Yajus-formulas; the initiations, all sacrifices, and the sacrificial rites; the sacrificial fees, the year, the sacrificer, and the worlds.
Where Soma flows clear and where the Sun is. || 2.1.6 ||
And from him the gods were produced in many ways—
the Sādhyas, humans, cattle, and birds; as well as inhalation and exhalation, rice and barley, and austerity.
Faith, truthfulness, celibacy, and ritual injunction. || 2.1.7 ||
From that, the seven vital breaths arise;
there are seven flames, seven fuels, and seven oblations. These are the seven worlds in which the vital breaths move.
Seven by seven are they deposited, dwelling in the cave.
From him all the oceans and mountains arise;
from him flow the rivers of every form;
and from him come all herbs and their essence.
By which this inner self indeed exists through the elements. || 2.1.9 ||
The Person alone is all this—the world, action, austerity, and the supreme immortal Brahman.
He who knows this, hidden in the secret cave of the heart, O dear one, unravels the knot of ignorance right here. 2.1.10.
Thus ends the first section.
Manifest, yet moving in secret, is that great station; therein all this is contained.
Know this as that which moves, breathes, and blinks—the existent and non-existent, the most excellent, higher than perception, and supreme among creatures. 2.2.1.
That which is radiant, subtler than the subtle, in which the worlds and the inhabitants of the worlds are contained—that is this imperishable Brahman; it is breath, it is speech, and it is mind.
That is truth, that is immortality; O dear one, know that this is what must be pierced through. 2.2.2.
Having taken up the great weapon of the Upaniṣads as the bow, one should fix the sharpened arrow of meditation;
drawing it back with a mind absorbed in that state of being.
Know that very thing to be the target, my dear, the Imperishable. 2.2.3.
The syllable Om is the bow, the self is indeed the arrow, and Brahman is said to be the target;
one must pierce it with undistracted mind, and like the arrow, become one with it. (2.2.4)
In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, along with the mind and all the vital breaths—
know him alone as the one Self; [abandon] other words.
Release your speech; this is the bridge to immortality. || 2.2.5 ||
Wherein the channels converge like the spokes in the hub of a wheel,
that very Self moves within, being born in many ways.
Meditate upon the Self as "Om" alone.
May there be well-being for you to reach the further shore beyond darkness. 2.2.6.
He who is omniscient and all-knowing, whose majesty is upon this earth—he, the Self, is established in the divine city of Brahman, in the ether. (2.2.7a)
Consisting of mind, leading the body of vital breaths, it is established in food, having placed its seat in the heart;
the wise behold it through discernment.
That which shines forth as the immortal form of bliss. || 2.2.7b ||
The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. (2.2.8)
In the supreme golden sheath is the stainless, partless Brahman;
that is the pure light of lights, which those who know the Self know. (2.2.9)
There the sun does not shine, nor do the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire.
Everything shines only after Him as He shines.
By its light all this shines. 2.2.10.
Brahman alone is this immortal reality in the east; Brahman is behind, Brahman is to the south and to the north; Brahman is spread out below and above.
Brahman alone is this universe, this most excellent.
Thus ends the second section.
Thus ends the second Muṇḍaka.
Two birds, united and companions, cling to the same tree;
of these two, one eats the sweet fruit.
The other looks on, not eating. 3.1.1.
On the same tree, a person is immersed and grieves, deluded by a lack of sovereignty;
but when he perceives the other, the Lord who is beloved, [he is freed].
"His majesty"—thus [one becomes] free from sorrow. 3.1.2.
When the seer beholds the golden-hued one,
the maker, the Lord, the Person whose source is Brahman,
then the wise man, having shaken off both merit and sin, [attains liberation].
Stainless, he attains supreme equality. 3.1.3.
For he is indeed the vital breath who shines forth through all beings;
the one who knows thus becomes a wise man who does not speak beyond [the truth].
He plays in the Self, rejoices in the Self, and is possessed of action.
He is the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman. || 3.1.4 ||
This Self is indeed to be attained through truth, through austerity, through perfect knowledge, and through constant celibacy;
for it is luminous and pure within the body.
That which ascetics, whose defects have been exhausted, behold.
Truth alone triumphs, not falsehood;
by truth is the path leading to the gods spread out,
by which the seers whose desires are fulfilled ascend.
Wherein lies that supreme treasure of truth. || 3.1.6 ||
It is vast and divine, of inconceivable form;
it shines forth as subtler than the subtlest.
It is far, yet very far away, and yet it is here in close proximity.
It is placed right here within the cave, even while they are looking.
It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech,
nor by other gods, nor by austerity or ritual action;
it is attained by one whose being is purified through the clarity of knowledge.
Then, meditating, he beholds that partless [reality].
This subtle self is to be known by the mind,
in which the vital breath has entered fivefold; by the vital breaths, the entire consciousness of living beings is woven.
When that [mind] is purified, this self becomes manifest. || 3.1.9 ||
Whatever world a pure being contemplates with the mind and whatever desires he longs for,
he conquers that very world and those very desires.
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should indeed honor the knower of the Self. 3.1.10.
Thus ends the first section.
He knows this supreme abode of Brahman, wherein the universe is placed and shines forth in splendor;
those who, free from desires, worship that Puruṣa.
Those wise ones transcend this semen. 3.2.1

He who, thinking them desirable, desires sensual pleasures, is born again and again among those very things by means of those desires; but for one whose desires are fulfilled and whose self is perfected, [there is no such rebirth].
Right here all desires dissolve away. (3.2.2)
This Self is not to be attained by instruction,
nor by intellect, nor by much hearing;
it is attained only by him whom this Self chooses.
To him, this Self reveals its own form. 3.2.3.
This Self is not attained by one who is devoid of strength,
nor through negligence, nor through austerity lacking the proper signs;
but the wise man who strives by means of these very methods—
His self enters that abode of Brahman. 3.2.4.
Having attained this, the sages— satisfied with knowledge, perfected in self, free from passion, and tranquil— being wise,
attain that which is all-pervading and omnipresent.
Those whose selves are disciplined enter into everything. 3.2.5.
Those ascetics of purified being, whose purpose has been well-ascertained through the higher knowledge of Vedānta and who have attained perfection through the yoga of renunciation—
they, at the time of the final end, [attain] the worlds of Brahman.
Having reached the supreme immortality, they are all completely liberated. || 3.2.6 ||
The fifteen parts have entered into their foundations,
and all the deities into their respective deities;
so too have the ritual acts and the self consisting of consciousness.
In the other, the imperishable, all become one. 3.2.7.
Just as rivers, flowing onward, reach their end in the ocean, casting off name and form,
so the knower, liberated from name and form, [reaches the Supreme].
He attains the divine Person who is higher than the high. || 3.2.8 ||

He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself. In his family, no one ignorant of Brahman is born. He crosses over sorrow, he crosses over evil; released from the knots of the heart, he becomes immortal. This very thing is expressed by a Rigvedic verse:
"The learned performers of rites, established in Brahman, themselves offering oblations with faith to the Single Seer..."
One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the "head-vow" has been performed according to the prescribed rule. (3.2.10)
This very truth the seer Aṅgiras spoke of old; one who has not observed the vows does not study this. Homage to the supreme seers! Homage to the supreme seers! 3.2.11
Thus ends the second section.
Thus ends the third Muṇḍaka.
Thus ends the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
